newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin hails Orthodox Church on Russian Easter.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin hails Orthodox Church on Russian Easter.

text.p: Millions of Russians celebrated Orthodox Easter on Sunday and President Boris Yeltsin said the influence of the Orthodox Church, recovering from decades of Soviet repression, was set to grow.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov attended a midnight service in the capital in a sign of the new close links between the Orthodox Church and Russia's secular leaders, many of them prominent former communists.

Regardless of their religious convictions, many Russians feel a deep cultural affinity with the 1,000-year-old Church and used the greeting "Christ has risen" on Sunday. "Indeed he has risen" is the expected reply.

In two separate messages issued at the very start of Easter day, when crowds of worshippers began candlelit processions around churches across Russia, Yeltsin praised the Church's contribution to the country's post-Soviet spiritual rebirth.

"The Russian Orthodox Church occupies a special place in the life of Russian society, in developing and strengthening its spiritual and moral values and in achieving civil peace and accord," he said in a message to Moscow Patriarch Alexiy.

"I am sure that fruitful cooperation between Russian state structures and the Orthodox Church will be further extended and strengthened," Yeltsin said, thanking the church for its charity work and contribution to the development of Russian culture.

The Patriarch said the restoration of churches in difficult economic times was a "miracle" and urged Muscovites to spread goodwill among the poor, sick and lonely. "Share an Easter egg, share a piece of Easter cake," he said on Ekho Moskvy radio.
He later celebrated mass at the capital's Christ the Saviour cathedral, now close to completion after just two years work to resurrect the 19th-century original destroyed by Stalin in 1931.
The Orthodox Church, hounded under communism, has undergone a vigorous revival since the old system collapsed in 1991, although an initial wave of public interest has subsided.
A survey among Muscovites by the All-Russia Centre for the Study of Public Opinion showed last week that 67 percent were believers but only four percent attended church every week.
But at the Bogoyavlenski Sobor (Epiphany Cathedral) in Moscow, crowds queued for hours to attend the prestigious Easter service conducted by the Patriarch.
Yeltsin, who normally goes to the church at Easter, was on holiday in the Black Sea resort of Sochi.
Police patrols were stepped up around the cathedral and officers with sniffer dogs searched the building for explosives.
In a technological breakthrough for the Church, the service was transmitted live over the Internet global computer network.
The Church was an integral part of the state before the 1917 Bolshevik revolution and is now keen to boost its role, although church leaders say they do not want a fusion with the state.
They say relations with members of other established faiths, including Moslems, Jews, Buddhists and Catholics, are good, but are concerned about fundamentalism and the spread of foreign sects.

Some representatives of other beliefs say there are sporadic cases of discrimination at a local level in favour of the Orthodox Church, whose strong historical and cultural roots have caught the imagination of Russian nationalists.
In his message to Orthodox Christians, Yeltsin appeared to address the concerns on both sides when he said cooperation between faiths was essential for civil and ethnic peace.

"I believe that all Russians, regardless of their religious convictions, will work together to ensure that this year...becomes an important landmark on the path of spiritual and moral renewal of our Fatherland," he said.
"I intend to further aid successful cooperation between the state and religious organisations, the consistent realisation of freedom of conscience and faith as laid down in the constitution."
